title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers
description: Brute force to optimized: re-sorting all eligible workers by quality for every candidate ratio versus a capped max-heap swept in ratio order.

sections.title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers

content.title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: There are n workers, each with a quality and a minimum wage expectation. Paying a group of hired workers must follow two rules: every worker in the group is paid in proportion to their quality, and every worker must be paid at least their minimum wage expectation. Given quality, wage, and an integer k, hire exactly k workers to form a group with the smallest possible total pay satisfying both rules.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every worker in a group must be paid at the SAME wage-to-quality ratio","The group's ratio is fixed by whichever worker demands the highest wage-to-quality ratio in that group"],["For a fixed ratio, cheaper total cost means minimizing total quality","A max-heap capped at size k, always keeping the k workers with smallest quality seen so far"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Pick exactly k workers to hire. All hired workers must be paid at a single common ratio of pay to quality, and that ratio must be at least each hired worker's own wage-to-quality ratio (their minimum acceptable rate). The total cost is that common ratio multiplied by the sum of the hired workers' qualities; find the group minimizing this total.

blocks.title: Analogy: Paying a Team Fairly at Everyone's Minimum Acceptable Rate
blocks.text: Picture assembling a team where everyone must be paid proportionally to their skill level, at a single shared rate. That shared rate must be at least high enough to satisfy the most demanding team member's own minimum rate, so picking a group with a lower "most demanding" rate, and lower total skill, keeps costs down.

blocks.caption: A group's ratio is fixed by its most demanding member; total cost = that ratio times total quality

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: quality = [10,20,5], wage = [70,50,30], k = 2
Worker 0 demands a ratio of 70/10 = 7; hiring workers 0 and 2 at ratio 7 costs 7 times (10 plus 5) = 105.00000.
The optimal group achieves a total cost of approximately 30.66667.
5. How Should We Think?
Before checking every possible group of k workers, notice that once a group's "most demanding" ratio is fixed, minimizing cost is purely about minimizing total quality among eligible workers.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If workers are considered in increasing order of their own wage-to-quality ratio, and a specific worker is treated as the group's most demanding member (the highest ratio allowed in the group), then every OTHER group member must have a ratio at most that value, meaning they can only be chosen from workers already considered.

Observation 2: For a FIXED most-demanding ratio, the cheapest possible group of k workers picks the k smallest-quality workers among those eligible (ratio at most the fixed one), since cost is ratio times total quality.

Observation 3: Sweeping workers in increasing ratio order, and maintaining a max-heap of quality capped at size k, always keeps exactly the k smallest-quality eligible workers seen so far, discarding the largest quality whenever the heap overflows.

Observation 4: Whenever the heap reaches exactly size k, the current worker's ratio times the heap's total quality is a valid candidate cost; the minimum across all such candidates is the answer.
This leads to sorting workers by their own ratio, then sweeping through them while maintaining a size-k max-heap of quality, computing a candidate cost every time the heap is full.
6. Brute Force Solution
Sort workers by ratio. For each worker treated as the group's most demanding member, freshly gather and sort every eligible worker by quality, take the k smallest, and compute the cost.
Step by step algorithm

items: Sort workers by their own wage-to-quality ratio, ascending.
For each worker i (0-indexed after sorting), consider it as the group's most demanding ratio.
Collect the qualities of workers 0 through i, sort them, and take the k smallest.
If at least k eligible workers exist, compute ratio[i] times their total quality, and track the minimum across every i.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: for each candidate max-ratio worker, freshly re-sort eligible workers by quality

codes.python:
def min_cost_to_hire_workers(quality, wage, k):
    n = len(quality)
    workers = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: wage[i] / quality[i])
    best = float('inf')
    for i in range(n):
        ratio = wage[workers[i]] / quality[workers[i]]
        eligible = sorted(quality[workers[j]] for j in range(i + 1))  # re-sort from scratch each time
        if len(eligible) >= k:
            cost = ratio * sum(eligible[:k])
            best = min(best, cost)
    return best

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Workers are sorted once by ratio up front, since that ordering determines which workers are eligible for each candidate group.
For every candidate max-ratio worker, the entire eligible set is re-sorted by quality from scratch, which is where the repeated work comes from.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), re-sorting up to n eligible workers by quality, for each of n candidate max-ratio workers.
Space: O(n) per candidate.

Limitation: the eligible set only ever grows by one worker at a time as i increases, but the brute force re-sorts it completely from scratch every time, instead of incrementally maintaining just the k smallest qualities seen so far.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-sorting the eligible set every time is wasteful: as i increases by one, only a single new worker's quality is added to the eligible set, the rest is unchanged.

What structure tracks "the k smallest qualities seen so far" incrementally: a max-heap capped at size k; push the new quality in, and if the heap now exceeds size k, pop the largest quality, since it is no longer among the k smallest.

The core idea: sweep workers in ratio order, maintaining a running sum of the k smallest qualities via a capped max-heap, and compute a candidate cost every time the heap reaches exactly size k.

Sort workers by ratio. Sweep through them, pushing each worker's quality onto a max-heap and adding it to a running quality sum. If the heap exceeds size k, pop the largest quality and subtract it from the sum. Whenever the heap holds exactly k workers, compute the current worker's ratio times the running quality sum as a candidate cost, tracking the minimum.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: sweep in ratio order, maintain a capped max-heap of quality

codes.python:
import heapq

def min_cost_to_hire_workers(quality, wage, k):
    n = len(quality)
    workers = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: wage[i] / quality[i])
    max_heap = []                          # negated values simulate a max-heap
    quality_sum = 0
    best = float('inf')
    for i in workers:
        ratio = wage[i] / quality[i]
        heapq.heappush(max_heap, -quality[i])
        quality_sum += quality[i]
        if len(max_heap) > k:
            quality_sum += heapq.heappop(max_heap)     # remove the largest quality (add back its negation)
        if len(max_heap) == k:
            best = min(best, ratio * quality_sum)
    return best

blocks.text: Why This Works

Sweeping workers in increasing ratio order guarantees that when a given worker is processed, every worker considered so far has a ratio at most the current one, exactly the eligibility rule. The capped max-heap always holds the k smallest qualities among those eligible workers, since any quality larger than the k smallest is popped out the moment the cap is exceeded, so the running quality sum is always exactly the minimum possible total quality for a valid group at the current ratio.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting once by ratio, then one heap push and at most one pop per worker.
Space: O(n) for the heap and sorted order.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem combines two ideas: fixing a group's "most demanding" ratio by sweeping candidates in sorted order, and maintaining the cheapest possible quality total for that ratio with a capped max-heap, rather than repeatedly re-sorting from scratch.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that the group's pay ratio must be at least the HIGHEST ratio among its own members, not an average or arbitrary choice.
Using a min-heap instead of a max-heap, which would keep the largest qualities instead of discarding them.
Computing a candidate cost before the heap has reached exactly size k.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explaining upfront why a group must be paid at its most demanding member's ratio, and why sweeping in ratio order combined with a capped heap finds the optimal group for every possible "most demanding" choice, shows the full reasoning clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how do you handle the shared-ratio constraint", think: sweep candidates in increasing ratio order, fixing each in turn as the group's most demanding member.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid re-sorting for every candidate", think: a max-heap capped at size k tracks the smallest-quality eligible workers incrementally.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if workers could be hired in fractional amounts (i.e., partial workers)?
How does this problem relate to other "fix one dimension, optimize the other with a heap" problems?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "sweep in sorted order of one dimension, maintain a capped heap for the other" optimization pattern.
IPO and similar greedy-plus-heap scheduling problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared log n) time; the optimized capped-heap sweep runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: sweep in sorted order of one dimension (ratio), maintaining a capped max-heap for the other (quality).
Core Idea: for each candidate "most demanding" ratio, the optimal group takes the k smallest-quality eligible workers, tracked incrementally with a size-k max-heap instead of re-sorting.
Time: O(n squared log n) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for both.
Most Important Observation: a group's pay ratio is always fixed by its most demanding member, letting every possible ratio be checked by a single sweep in sorted order.
Interview Difficulty: requires recognizing both the ratio-sweep framing and the capped-heap technique together.
One line memory trick: sweep by ratio, keep the k smallest qualities in a capped max-heap.
